title: The prayer of the heart
hook: bring the mind down into the heart and stand before God

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last stop with the Benedictines: lectio in the cloister. Your line was chew it slowly. Which word of your verse kept coming back? Day one thousand one hundred twenty.

Go down with your mind into your heart, and stand there before God. That's the advice, in substance, of a Russian bishop and hermit the Orthodox church remembers as Saint Theophan the Recluse. Tradition says he gave it to people who wrote to him asking how to pray. Not louder. Not longer. Lower. We leave the Benedictine cloister today and cross into another room in the house: the Orthodox way of the heart. Tradition counts desert monks and forest hermits among its teachers. And their first lesson is a direction, almost a map. Attention tends to live up in the head, busy and chattering. Bring it down. Today's word: the prayer of the heart.

Start with what the Bible means by heart. It's not only where feelings live. In scripture the heart is the center of a person: where you think, decide, remember, love. After the shepherds' visit, Luke says, "Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." Pondering, there, is heart work. And Jesus says, "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God." Seeing God, and the heart, in one breath. The Orthodox teachers take that seriously. If the heart is the center, then prayer that stays in the head stays on the surface. Words said, thoughts thought, while the real you is somewhere else. So they teach a descent. The mind, the busy attention, comes down and rests in the heart, the way a bird that's been beating around a room finally settles on a perch. And there, still, you stand before God. Not explaining yourself. Not performing. Just present. Some who walk this way use a short prayer, said slowly over and over, often in rhythm with the breath. One form of it runs: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. It's called the Jesus Prayer, and it echoes what the blind man and the tax collector say in the Gospels. Jesus himself gives a picture of the place: "when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." Some Orthodox teachers hear the closet as the heart. Go in. Shut the door. Pray there.

Here's the practice: rest your attention in your chest. Sit upright, feet on the floor. Notice where your attention is right now; it may be somewhere behind your eyes. Let it sink, slowly, down your throat, to the middle of your chest. Feel your breath there, rising and falling. When a thought pulls you back up, notice, and let the attention sink again. If you pray, you can say the Jesus Prayer quietly with the breath. If not, just rest there. The bell holds the time.
The prayer of the heart. In the Orthodox tradition, prayer where the mind comes down into the heart and stands before God.

howItsDone: In Orthodox Christianity, monks, nuns and lay people practice the prayer of the heart, often by repeating the Jesus Prayer slowly, sometimes with a prayer rope, under the guidance of a spiritual father or mother.

notes: Theophan's 'descend with the mind into the heart and stand before the face of the Lord' is paraphrased; the familiar English wording is from a modern (copyrighted) anthology. Confirm the attribution and the description of him as bishop and recluse, and that he wrote letters of direction.
'Tradition counts desert monks and forest hermits among its teachers. is a general description not in the cited text; confirm or soften.
'Some who walk this way use a short prayer' and 'its usual words' describe the Jesus Prayer; the wording varies (some add 'a sinner'). 'Some' used, no count claimed.
The Jesus Prayer described, not newly written. Linked to Mark 10:47 (the blind man) and Luke 18:13 (the tax collector) as echoes, not as sources.
Reading the 'closet' of Matthew 6:6 as the heart is attributed to 'the Orthodox teachers'; confirm.
Sub-block boundary: first day of 'The Orthodox way of the heart'.

Editor pass: Luke 2 names a manger, not a stable, so 'leave the stable' became 'after the shepherds' visit'; fixed the garbled bird on a branch inside a room; 'usual words' and 'the Orthodox teachers' softened to 'one form' and 'some'; no longer tells the listener where their attention is.
Audit pass: no change. Luke 2:19, Matthew 5:8, Matthew 6:6 exact KJV; Theophan paraphrased and hedged; the heart's definition no longer duplicates day 1112.
